# A. Safe Region Diameter

## How to find it

First recover the convex intersection polygon with the half-plane deque. Then
use rotating calipers to find its farthest pair of vertices.

## Correctness

The deque produces exactly the feasible polygon. A diameter of a convex polygon
has antipodal endpoints; rotating calipers enumerates every antipodal pair while
the opposite pointer moves only forward, so the largest tested distance is the
region diameter.

## Complexity

`O(n log n)` time for sorting half-planes plus `O(h)` calipers time, and `O(n)`
memory.

# B. Round Table Clearance

## How to find it

Offset every counterclockwise edge inward by radius `r`; exploit the convex polygon edge order for a linear deque feasibility test, then binary-search `r`.

## Correctness

A center supports radius `r` exactly when its distance from every edge is at least `r`. The deque finds a candidate intersection in edge order, and the final all-edge witness check certifies that candidate before declaring feasibility.

## Complexity

`O(n log precision)` time and `O(n)` memory.

# C. Sensor Overlap

## How to find it

Separate disjoint and containment cases before using the two-sector lens formula.

## Correctness

In the proper-overlap case the common region partitions into two sectors minus their center triangles; the other classifications are immediate.

## Complexity

`O(1)` time and memory.

# D. Emergency Broadcast Disk

## How to find it

Randomize insertion order and rebuild only when a point violates the current circle, fixing one, two, then three boundary witnesses.

## Correctness

At every nesting level the violating fixed points must lie on the new optimum boundary; one to three such points uniquely determine the minimum circle for the processed prefix.

## Complexity

Expected `O(n)` time and `O(n)` storage.

# E. Delaunay Route

## How to find it

Build the Delaunay edges, weight them by Euclidean length, and run Dijkstra from
the requested source site.

## Correctness

The construction returns exactly the graph permitted by the statement.
Euclidean edge lengths are nonnegative, so Dijkstra's settled-distance
invariant gives the shortest permitted route.

## Complexity

Expected `O(n squared)` for the local incremental triangulation, followed by
`O(n log n)` shortest-path work on the linear-size Delaunay graph.

# F. Low-Cost Fiber

## How to find it

Build Delaunay edges and run Kruskal on that sparse graph.

## Correctness

Every Euclidean MST edge has an empty-disk certificate and belongs to Delaunay, so discarding all other complete-graph edges preserves an optimum.

## Complexity

Expected `O(n squared + n log n)` here.
